techniques.name: Persistent spatial bus graph (panners + buses live forever; only sources are one-shot)
techniques.howItWorks: The expensive, stateful nodes — a per-category submix GainNode, the StereoPanner/PannerNode, the air-absorption lowpass, the reverb ConvolverNode and its send — are built ONCE at unlock and kept alive for the life of the AudioContext. Only the cheap, fire-and-forget primitives (OscillatorNode, AudioBufferSourceNode of the shared noise buffer) are created per cue, started, and self-stop. This is THE correct Web Audio idiom: buffer sources are 'one-time-use-only, fire-and-forget' and cannot be pooled or rewound, but the topology around them can and should be permanent. The current code rebuilds a fresh Gain+StereoPanner+Biquad per cue and tears them down with setTimeout — that churn is the thing to eliminate.
techniques.webAudioMapping: Build at unlock: masterGain -> compressor(glue) -> destination. Under master, a fixed set of category buses (smallarms, he, atmos, net) each a GainNode. Each bus splits into a DRY path (-> master) and a WET send GainNode -> the single shared ConvolverNode -> master. Per cue, create only osc/noise sources, connect them to a tiny per-cue envelope GainNode, connect THAT to the right bus's input and (scaled) to the bus's wet send. The per-cue env gain is genuinely cheap to create; the panner/convolver/compressor are not. Keep a small free-list of env GainNodes if even that churn shows up in profiling.
techniques.source: padenot 'Web Audio API performance and debugging notes' (GainNode cheap to create; ConvolverNode/HRTF very expensive) https://padenot.github.io/web-audio-perf/ ; W3C/MDN on AudioBufferSourceNode one-shot design

techniques.name: Keep StereoPanner, NOT HRTF PannerNode, for the top-down tactical listener
techniques.howItWorks: HRTF panningModel runs a continuous convolution against measured head impulse responses per source, and on a MOVING source cross-fades between old/new position — up to four convolvers per stereo voice at once. With a 24-voice firefight cap this is the single most expensive thing you could do, and HRTF buys you front/back + elevation discrimination that a TOP-DOWN map view does not need and cannot honestly portray (there is no 'in front of / behind the player' — the player is a disembodied overhead eye). HRTF also colors/phase-smears badly on loudspeakers (it is tuned for headphones). equalpower PannerNode is 'rather cheap' but still does vector math per source; StereoPanner is cheaper still because you already have the screen-space pan and skip the vector math entirely.
techniques.webAudioMapping: Keep the existing StereoPannerNode per category bus (or per voice). Compute pan exactly as today: pan = clamp((dx*ppm)/(vw/2), -1, 1). Do NOT switch to PannerNode+HRTF. If you ever want the listener-orientation API for free distance math, use PannerNode with panningModel:'equalpower' and distanceModel handled by the panner — but for a fixed top-down camera the hand-rolled StereoPanner+distance you have is both faster and more controllable. Reserve HRTF only behind an explicit 'headphone mode' toggle if ever desired.
techniques.source: MDN PannerNode.panningModel (HRTF = convolution, higher cost) https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/PannerNode/panningModel ; padenot perf notes (HRTF 'Very expensive', up to 4 convolvers; equalpower cheap; StereoPanner cheapest) https://padenot.github.io/web-audio-perf/

techniques.name: Terrain LOS occlusion: ridge-line blocks high frequencies, not volume (the 'fire from the next draw' muffle)
techniques.howItWorks: Real combat audio in a Korengal-type valley is dominated by terrain masking: a PKM firing from behind a spur sounds dull and bass-heavy, then snaps bright the instant it has line-of-sight to you. Game audio models this exactly as game engines do — raycast listener->source; if terrain intersects, drive an occlusion factor 0..1 that LOWERS a lowpass cutoff and applies modest volume reduction. You already have the ground truth (terrain.elevAt) to march a profile between camera-center and the cue position and test whether the straight sight-line clears the ridge. This is the highest-immersion-per-line technique available to this specific game because the valley IS the enemy.
techniques.webAudioMapping: Per positional cue, sample N=~12 points along the segment cam-center -> cue.pos, compute the straight-line sight elevation vs terrain.elevAt at each; occ = fraction of samples where terrain rises above the line (or max penetration depth normalized). Map occ to the per-cue air-absorption BiquadFilter (lowpass) you ALREADY have: cutoff = lerp(currentNearCutoff, 350Hz, occ) and gain *= lerp(1.0, 0.5, occ) (~ -6 dB, less than the -15 dB indoor figure because rock diffraction still passes a lot). Because the mapper must stay pure/deterministic, do the raycast render-side in player.spatial() using the live terrain handle — it's already non-deterministic-safe there (ctx.currentTime lives there too). Smooth occ per source toward target (lerp ~5/s) to avoid pops as the ridge edge crosses.
techniques.source: raduacg game-mechanics-optimizations 112_audio_occlusion (raycast 10-30Hz, cutoff 20k->300Hz, up to -15dB, smooth lerp) https://github.com/raduacg/game-mechanics-optimizations/blob/main/112_audio_occlusion.md ; CryEngine/FMOD occlusion=lowpass+volume mapping; SoundCy/SciAm on terrain scatter softening gunfire https://soundcy.com/article/what-does-shooting-sound-like

techniques.name: Elevation brightness cue: enemy on the high ground reads as BRIGHTER/more present
techniques.howItWorks: Human elevation perception is driven by spectral peaks/notches above ~4 kHz (most pronounced 6-9 kHz) imposed by the pinna — you literally cannot pan elevation with L/R level. In a top-down view you can't render true elevation HRTF, but you CAN encode the firing-from-above relationship the player needs to FEEL: a gun on the ridge firing down has clear line-of-sight and an unobstructed high-frequency path, so it should be brighter and slightly closer-sounding than a same-distance gun in the valley floor (which is partly terrain-masked). This converts an unrenderable cue (azimuth-of-elevation) into a renderable, doctrinally-correct one (the high gun is the dangerous, present one — 'we're getting shot at from up there').
techniques.webAudioMapping: Compute relElev = terrain.elevAt(cue.pos) - terrain.elevAt(cam.center). Add a persistent high-shelf BiquadFilter (type:'highshelf', freq ~5000Hz) on the smallarms bus or per cue, gain = clamp(relElev/heightScale, -1, 1) * +/-4 dB (boost when source is above listener, cut when below). Pair with a small distance-perception nudge: when relElev>0, reduce the wet/reverb send a touch (high ground = direct path) and raise the air-absorption cutoff ~15% so the high gun sits forward in the mix. Keep it subtle — 3-4 dB — to stay restrained, not arcade-y.
techniques.source: Nature/Sci Reports 'Spectral Weighting Underlies Perceived Sound Elevation' (elevation = spectral cues >4kHz, 6-9kHz band) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6367479/ ; J Neurosci pinna elevation cues https://www.jneurosci.org/content/30/1/194

techniques.name: Procedural valley reverb via decaying-noise ConvolverNode IR (no audio asset)
techniques.howItWorks: The classic Moorer result is that exponentially-decaying filtered white noise makes a surprisingly convincing reverb impulse response. You render such a buffer ONCE at startup into a ConvolverNode and get the long, ragged tail that defines mountain-valley gunfire — the 'echoes rolling in over seconds' that every Restrepo/Outpost firefight has and that this sim currently completely lacks. This is the single biggest believability jump available, and it is explicitly allowed by the constraints (the IR is procedurally generated, not shipped).
techniques.webAudioMapping: At unlock, build the IR with OfflineAudioContext(2, sampleRate*T, sampleRate): fill a stereo buffer with noise, apply env e^(-k*t/T) (T~1.6-2.2s for a tight valley; longer = bigger bowl), shape with highpass(~400Hz)+lowpass(~5kHz) so the tail is dark and dirt-like not hissy, add a few discrete early-reflection taps (DelayNodes 30-90ms at -8 to -12 dB) for the first slap off the opposite wall. Load into a single shared ConvolverNode. Wet/dry per source = distance: dryGain ~ atten, wetSend ~ atten * (0.15 + 0.5*norm) so FAR events are proportionally wetter ('loss of HF + more reverb = farther' is the core depth cue). One convolver shared by all 24 voices keeps cost flat — convolution is per-input-block expensive, so never one-convolver-per-voice.
techniques.source: gskinner 'Making Reverb with the Web Audio API' (OfflineAudioContext decaying noise IR, hp500/lp5k, multitap early reflections, wet/dry=distance) https://blog.gskinner.com/archives/2019/02/reverb-web-audio-api.html ; reverbGen / Moorer 'About This Reverberation Business' https://github.com/adelespinasse/reverbGen ; SciAm gunfire echo 'smear' https://www.scientificamerican.com/blog/cocktail-party-physics/a-shot-in-the-dark-the-acoustics-of-gunfire/

techniques.name: Distance = wet/dry depth bus, not just attenuation (loss-of-HF + more reverb)
techniques.howItWorks: The ear's primary distance cues are (1) loss of high frequency and (2) increased reverb-to-direct ratio — NOT just lower volume. The current system has the HF-loss half (the air-absorption lowpass) but no reverb, so far events read as 'quiet near events' rather than 'distant'. Adding a per-source wet send scaled UP with distance completes the cue and makes the existing crack-thump split land properly (you hear the dry crack pan-located, then the wet thump bloom out of the valley).
techniques.webAudioMapping: Reuse the existing 0..1 'norm' distance from spatial(). dryGain = atten (as today). wetSend = atten * clamp(0.12 + 0.55*norm, 0, 0.7) into the shared ConvolverNode. Keep the existing air-absorption lowpass as the HF-loss half. For the crack-thump pair specifically, route the bright CRACK mostly dry+panned and the low THUMP with a heavier wet send so the report 'rolls' — this is exactly the perceptual 'flash then thunder' beat.
techniques.source: Sage Audio / gearspace on reverb-as-distance (wetter=farther, HF loss cues distance) https://www.sageaudio.com/blog/mixing/how-to-create-depth-and-width-with-reverb-and-delay.php ; Audiokinetic Reverb Zones https://www.audiokinetic.com/en/blog/fun-with-reverb-zones/

techniques.name: DynamicsCompressorNode glue bus + priority voice-stealing for the 24-cap
techniques.howItWorks: When 30 men are firing, summing 24 unclamped voices clips hard and turns to mush. A DynamicsCompressorNode on the master sums-and-tames the peaks ('lowers the loudest parts to prevent clipping when multiple sounds multiplex'). Pair it with smarter voice management than the current 'drop whatever arrives after 24': implement priority voice-stealing — an IED/blast or a near, loud cue should steal a slot from a distant rifle crack, not be silently dropped. Game audio voice priority is classically driven by amplitude (post-distance gain) + a per-kind importance weight.
techniques.webAudioMapping: Insert a DynamicsCompressorNode between master and destination (threshold ~ -10dB, ratio ~4, fast-ish attack ~3ms, release ~120ms) as the glue bus. For voice mgmt: compute each pending cue's priority = KIND_TRIM[kind]*importance + sp.gain (louder/closer/bigger wins). When at MAX_VOICES, if an incoming cue outranks the current quietest active voice, fade-and-reclaim it (short 15-25ms gain ramp to 0 then disconnect) instead of dropping the new one. Track active voices with their priority so stealing is O(1)-ish on a tiny sorted ring.
techniques.source: MDN/W3C DynamicsCompressorNode (prevents clipping when multiplexing many sounds; GainNode summing junction for buses) https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_Audio_API ; classic game-audio voice-stealing-by-amplitude+priority (Unity/Wwise/FMOD doctrine) https://feedback.unity3d.com/suggestions/increase-audio-voice-polyphony-t

techniques.name: Distance model choice if you ever adopt PannerNode: inverse + rolloffFactor>=2
techniques.howItWorks: If you migrate distance handling to a PannerNode instead of the hand-rolled pow() falloff, use distanceModel:'inverse' (best approximates the real inverse-square law and never hard-cuts to silence) with rolloffFactor 2-3; linear with the default maxDistance 10000 effectively ignores distance, and inverse/exponential are identical at rolloffFactor 1 so you MUST raise it to get audible falloff. Note your current hand-rolled pow((1-norm),1.6) with a zoom-scaled AUDIBLE_M is actually MORE controllable for a zoom-dependent audible radius than the panner's fixed-meter model, so this is a fallback, not a recommendation to switch.
techniques.webAudioMapping: Only if switching to PannerNode: panningModel:'equalpower', distanceModel:'inverse', refDistance scaled to your zoom (e.g. halfW), rolloffFactor ~2.5, maxDistance ~ AUDIBLE_M. Otherwise keep the existing hand-rolled atten = pow(max(0,1-norm),1.6) which already gives you zoom-coupled audibility the panner can't easily replicate.
techniques.source: Kieran Farr 'Understanding Web Audio Positional Audio Distance Models for WebXR' (inverse recommended, rolloff 2-3, linear@default ignores distance, inverse==exp at rolloff 1) https://medium.com/@kfarr/understanding-web-audio-api-positional-audio-distance-models-for-webxr-e77998afcdff ; MDN PannerNode.distanceModel https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/PannerNode/distanceModel

techniques.name: Throttle occlusion/elevation raycasts to ~15-20 Hz, cache per source, cull cheap
techniques.howItWorks: Terrain raycasts are the one new per-cue cost that could blow the frame budget in a 30-man fight. Engines run occlusion checks at 10-30 Hz (NOT per frame), cache the result, and skip the check entirely for sources below a volume threshold or beyond max distance. Because your cues are mostly transient one-shots (a rifle crack lasts 100ms), most cues only need ONE raycast at schedule time — the expensive case is sustained/repeated fire from a fixed position, which you can key/cache by quantized source position.
techniques.webAudioMapping: Cull first: if atten<0.02 (already done) skip the raycast entirely. For repeated fire from the same grid cell, cache occ/relElev keyed by floor(pos.x/5),floor(pos.y/5) with a ~50ms TTL so a SAW rip's burst-of-cracks reuses one raycast. Keep the march coarse (8-12 samples) — sub-cell precision is inaudible. This keeps the added cost to a few hundred elevAt() lookups per frame even in a firefight, well within budget since elevAt is a bilinear sample, not a full LOS algorithm.
techniques.source: raduacg audio_occlusion (10-30Hz checks, cache, skip <-40dB / >50m) https://github.com/raduacg/game-mechanics-optimizations/blob/main/112_audio_occlusion.md ; padenot perf notes (avoid per-frame heavy work) https://padenot.github.io/web-audio-perf/

techniques.name: Use modern AudioListener AudioParams (positionX/forwardX), feature-detect for Firefox
techniques.howItWorks: setPosition()/setOrientation() on AudioListener and PannerNode are deprecated in favor of the .positionX/.forwardX/.upX AudioParams, which additionally support sample-accurate automation (linearRampToValueAtTime) — useful if you ever want the listener to glide with a camera pan rather than jump. Firefox historically only supported the deprecated methods, so feature-detect. This only matters if you adopt PannerNode/AudioListener; with pure StereoPanner the listener is implicit and this is moot.
techniques.webAudioMapping: If using AudioListener: if ('positionX' in listener) { listener.positionX.value = camX; listener.forwardZ.value = -1; ... } else { listener.setPosition(...); listener.setOrientation(0,0,-1,0,1,0); }. For smooth camera follow, listener.positionX.linearRampToValueAtTime(camX, ctx.currentTime+frameDt). With StereoPanner-only (recommended), skip entirely.
techniques.source: MDN AudioListener (setPosition/setOrientation deprecated -> positionX/forwardX AudioParams; Firefox bug 1283029) https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AudioListener ; servo/servo#22898

keyInsights: The biggest immersion win on this axis is NOT better panning — it's REVERB. The sim currently has zero reverberation; a procedurally-generated decaying-noise ConvolverNode IR gives the valley its signature 'echoes rolling in over seconds,' which is the one acoustic fingerprint of every Restrepo/Outpost firefight and is explicitly allowed (the IR is generated, no asset shipped).

For a TOP-DOWN listener, HRTF PannerNode is the wrong tool: it's the most expensive node in Web Audio (up to 4 convolvers per moving stereo voice), it's tuned for headphones and smears on speakers, and it buys front/back+elevation discrimination a disembodied overhead camera can't honestly use. Keep the cheap hand-rolled StereoPanner; spend the saved CPU on reverb + occlusion instead.

Terrain occlusion is THIS game's killer feature — 'the valley is the enemy' applies to sound too. You already own the ground truth (terrain.elevAt) to ray-march a sight-line and muffle a gun firing from behind a spur (lowpass down to ~350Hz + ~-6dB), then snap it bright the instant it has LOS. No other top-down shooter has terrain-masked audio because most don't have elevation data; you do.

Distance is wet/dry + HF-loss, not just volume. The current air-absorption lowpass is half the cue; adding a distance-scaled reverb SEND completes it so far events read as 'distant,' not 'quiet near.' This also makes the existing crack-thump split finally land: dry panned crack, then a wet thump that blooms out of the valley.

The right Web Audio architecture is a PERMANENT bus/panner/convolver/compressor topology with only the cheap osc/noise SOURCES created per cue. The current per-cue Gain+StereoPanner+Biquad churn (and setTimeout teardown) is exactly the allocation pattern padenot warns against; buffer sources are one-shot by design but everything downstream of them should live for the whole session.

Elevation can't be panned in 2D, so encode the relationship the PLAYER needs instead: a gun on the high ground (relElev>0) reads brighter (high-shelf +3-4dB, less reverb, clear LOS) — doctrinally correct ('getting shot at from up there') and grounded in real elevation perception being a >4kHz spectral cue, not a level cue.
pitfalls: Do NOT switch all 24 voices to HRTF PannerNode 'for realism' — it's the single most expensive choice in Web Audio (continuous convolution, up to 4 convolvers per moving stereo source) and will starve a 30-man firefight; it also colors badly on loudspeakers. HRTF buys elevation/front-back that a top-down camera cannot use.

Never instantiate one ConvolverNode (or one HRTF panner) per voice — convolution cost is per-input-block. Use ONE shared convolver fed by per-source wet sends; one shared noise AudioBuffer; persistent panners/buses.

Determinism trap: any raycast/occlusion/elevation math MUST stay render-side (in player.spatial(), where ctx.currentTime already lives) and never feed back into lib/sim. The mapper/cue layer must remain a pure function — do not read terrain into the cue.

Don't pop the filters: occlusion and elevation factors must lerp toward their target (~5/s) as the ridge edge crosses the sight-line, or you get audible clicks every time a soldier moves behind cover. Same for voice-stealing — fade out the stolen voice over 15-25ms, never hard-disconnect a sounding node.

Don't let reverb turn the 'readable silence of the calm-before' into a wash — gate the convolver's contribution to actual events (it already is, since no event = no source), keep T~1.6-2.2s not cathedral-length, and dark-filter the IR (hp400/lp5k) so the tail is dirt/rock, not a concert hall. Over-wet = arcade-y, the exact failure mode to avoid.

Linear distanceModel with the default maxDistance 10000 effectively ignores distance (sound seems non-positional); inverse==exponential at rolloffFactor 1. If you ever adopt PannerNode you must set inverse + rolloff>=2 — but the existing zoom-coupled hand-rolled falloff is actually better for this game's variable audible radius, so prefer keeping it.

Don't raycast per-frame per-voice — at 24 voices in a firefight that's a frame-budget hazard. Throttle to 15-20Hz, cache by quantized source cell with a short TTL (so a SAW rip's burst reuses one raycast), and cull before raycasting (the atten<0.02 cull already exists — keep it as the first gate).

Keep the elevation high-shelf and occlusion attenuation SUBTLE (3-6 dB). Rock diffraction passes a lot of low end even with no LOS, so the indoor -15dB occlusion figure is too aggressive for an open valley; over-muffling makes distant fire vanish unrealistically.

techniques.name: HDR window auto-mixer (compute-side, deterministic)
techniques.howItWorks: DICE's HDR audio model: every cue carries a notional loudness in dB-SPL-at-listener. A virtual 'window' of fixed Size (e.g. 35-40 dB) floats so its TOP tracks the loudest sound currently audible (an exponential release pulls it back down over ReleaseTime, e.g. 0.5-1.5 s). Anything whose loudness falls below the window BOTTOM is inaudible and is simply not scheduled. The window->output mapping then linearly remaps [bottom,top] dB to the playable amplitude range. Net effect: a near M4 raises the window so distant impacts/footsteps vanish, then as the firing stops the window sinks and the valley's small sounds re-emerge. This is the single mechanism that delivers BOTH legibility ('every sound is important, but not at the same time') and the somber 'readable calm-before' — silence is what the window decays into. Crucially it can run entirely in the pure mapper as a function of cue loudness, keeping it deterministic; only the final gain hits Web Audio.
techniques.webAudioMapping: No new nodes — it's gain math done before scheduling. Give each CueKind a loudnessDb constant (replace/augment KIND_TRIM, e.g. ied 128, blast_large 120, mg 105, muzzle 100, impact 75, ricochet 70, footstep/ambient 45). Maintain windowTop in the player (or mapper render-state): on each cue windowTop = max(windowTop, loudnessDb); each frame windowTop += (windowBottom_floor - windowTop) * (1 - exp(-dt/releaseTau)). windowBottom = windowTop - SIZE. For each cue: if loudnessDb < windowBottom -> cull (don't allocate the voice — this is also your over-budget pre-filter). Else outGain = pow(10, (loudnessDb - windowTop)/20) folded into the existing cueGain.gain.value (so the loudest sits at 0 dBFS-ref and quiet sounds get pushed down or out). Pairs with the distance attenuation already in spatial(): subtract distance dB from loudnessDb so a far gunshot can fall under the window of a near one.
techniques.source: Anders Clerwall (EA/DICE), 'How High Dynamic Range Audio Makes Battlefield: Bad Company Go BOOM', GDC 2009 — https://www.slideshare.net/aclerwall/how-high-dynamic-range-audio-makes-battlefield-bad-company-go-boom-1292018 ; concept writeup https://designingsound.org/2013/06/21/finding-your-way-with-high-dynamic-range-audio-in-wwise/

techniques.name: DynamicsCompressorNode master limiter (anti-clip safety net)
techniques.howItWorks: A single DynamicsCompressorNode on the master bus catches the peaks a 30-man firefight inevitably stacks (the current graph sums every voice into one GainNode with NO limiter, so a coincident MG burst + IED can hard-clip). Configured as a brickwall-ish limiter — low threshold, hard knee, high ratio, fast attack — it transparently tames transients so the mix stays legible and never distorts, while the HDR window above does the musical 'who matters' decision. The limiter is the dumb safety net; the HDR window is the smart mix. Watch its read-only .reduction to drive a 'mix is hot' meter or auto-trim.
techniques.webAudioMapping: Insert ONE node between master and destination: const lim = ctx.createDynamicsCompressor(); lim.threshold.value=-6; lim.knee.value=0; lim.ratio.value=20; lim.attack.value=0.003; lim.release.value=0.25; master.connect(lim).connect(ctx.destination). Defaults are threshold -24/knee 30/ratio 12/attack 0.003/release 0.25 — override threshold/knee/ratio for limiting. Keep master gain so typical peaks sit ~ -6 dBFS to leave the limiter headroom and avoid constant pumping. Note: the WebAudio compressor has makeup/lookahead quirks and can overshoot on very fast transients (IED) — keep its threshold conservative and rely on per-cue HDR gains to do most of the level work, not the limiter.
techniques.source: MDN DynamicsCompressorNode — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/DynamicsCompressorNode ; W3C Web Audio 1.1 — https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio-1.1/

techniques.name: Submix bus architecture (combat / atmos / radio / score)
techniques.howItWorks: Route every voice through a category bus GainNode before the master, instead of all-to-one. Buses: COMBAT (muzzle/mg/blast/ied/impact/ricochet/nearmiss/splash), ATMOS (smoke_pop/frag_air/flare + any future wind/bird bed), RADIO (radio squelch/beep), SCORE (tic_sting + future music). Buses are the levers that make ducking, mix-states, and per-category loudness trivial — you ramp ONE gain to duck a whole category. They also let you apply category-specific processing (e.g. a bandpass + bitcrush WaveShaper permanently on the RADIO bus for the comms 'small speaker' timbre; a touch of the convolution reverb only on COMBAT for the valley tail). This is the structural prerequisite for every other technique here.
techniques.webAudioMapping: Replace the single master with: per-bus const combatBus=ctx.createGain(), atmosBus, radioBus, scoreBus; each .connect(master); master.connect(limiter).connect(destination). schedule() routes cueGain.connect(lp).connect(pan).connect(BUS_FOR[cue.kind]) using a Record<CueKind,GainNode> map. Static bus trims set the somber balance: combatBus ~0 dB ref, atmosBus -6, radioBus -3 (under the log line), scoreBus -9. The RADIO bus gets a fixed chain radioBus = gain -> bandpass(center 1.6kHz, Q 1.2) -> waveshaper(mild tanh) -> master for the 'in the handset' color, built once.
techniques.source: DICE HDR talk (bus + priority categories); vndev.wiki 'Balancing a Game's Loudness' — https://vndev.wiki/Guide:Balancing_a_Game's_Loudness

techniques.name: Control-side ducking via setTargetAtTime bus envelopes (sidechain substitute)
techniques.howItWorks: Web Audio's DynamicsCompressorNode CANNOT be sidechained (no external trigger input) — true audio-rate sidechain needs an AudioWorklet, which would also break determinism and add cost. The correct, cheap, deterministic substitute is CONTROL-side ducking: when a ducking trigger occurs (radio cue scheduled, or a big blast), ramp the TARGET bus's gain down then back up with two setTargetAtTime calls (attack + release time-constants). 'Radio ducks atmos+combat slightly so the squelch reads'; 'an IED ducks EVERYTHING for ~250 ms then recovers over ~1.2 s — the felt-it-in-the-chest pressure-dump.' Because the duck amount and timing are a pure function of which cue fired, it stays deterministic. setTargetAtTime is click-free (exponential approach) and self-chains (next ramp starts from the live value), so overlapping ducks compose cleanly.
techniques.webAudioMapping: duck(bus, amount, attackTau, releaseTau, now): bus.gain.cancelScheduledValues(now); bus.gain.setTargetAtTime(baseGain*amount, now, attackTau); bus.gain.setTargetAtTime(baseGain, now+holdS, releaseTau). RADIO trigger: duck atmosBus to 0.5 & combatBus to 0.7, attackTau 0.02, hold 0.15, releaseTau 0.25. IED/blast_large trigger: duck atmosBus+radioBus+scoreBus to ~0.25 and combatBus to ~0.5, attackTau 0.004 (near-instant), hold 0.18, releaseTau 0.4-1.2 (the long swell back = the ears 'recovering'). Use time-CONSTANTS not ramps so it never clicks; cancelScheduledValues+anchor avoids fighting a prior duck. Pair the IED duck with a short scoreBus tinnitus tone for the deafened beat (see below).
techniques.source: MDN AudioParam.setTargetAtTime — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AudioParam/setTargetAtTime ; 'Web Audio: the ugly click and the human ear' — http://alemangui.github.io/ramp-to-value ; W3C issue #246 (no native sidechain) — https://github.com/WebAudio/web-audio-api/issues/246 ; soundbank-dipper — https://github.com/mmckegg/soundbank-dipper

techniques.name: Priority-weighted voice stealing (keep nearest+loudest, drop quietest)
techniques.howItWorks: The current cap drops the NEWEST cue once 24 voices are live ('continue' in the loop) — which can mute the very gunshot the player needs to hear while a stale ricochet keeps playing. Conventional game-audio prioritization instead computes a priority score per pending voice and, when over budget, culls the LOWEST-priority (quietest / most distant / least important) — and may STEAL an already-playing low-priority voice for a high-priority new one. DICE uses discrete classes (None/Low/Medium/High/Permanent); Unity falls back to audibility (louder wins) when class ties. Result: in a 30-man fight you always hear the closest weapons and the IED, and the carpet of distant impacts is what gets sacrificed — exactly the HDR philosophy enforced at the voice-budget layer.
techniques.webAudioMapping: Before scheduling, sort the frame's cues by priority = classWeight[cue.kind]*1000 + postHDRgain*100 (HDR gain already encodes distance+loudness). classWeight: ied/dangerclose/tic_sting = Permanent(4); blast/mg/splash = High(3); muzzle/radio = Medium(2); impact/ricochet/nearmiss/smoke = Low(1). Fill voices high->low; when activeVoices>=MAX_VOICES, if the new cue outranks the lowest live voice, tear that voice down (its existing setTimeout cleanup + a 5ms gain ramp to 0 to avoid a click) and take its slot; else cull the new cue. Track live voices in an array with {priority, cleanup} instead of just a counter. Raise MAX_VOICES to ~32 (Unity's default) now that HDR pre-culls and the limiter protects the sum.
techniques.source: Unity voice prioritization / gamedevbeginner audio optimization — https://gamedevbeginner.com/unity-audio-optimisation-tips/ ; Audiokinetic 'How to get a hold on your voices' — https://www.audiokinetic.com/en/blog/how-to-get-a-hold-on-your-voices-optimizing-for-cpu-part-1/ ; DICE HDR priority classes

techniques.name: Mix-states by intensity (calm / contact / overwhelm)
techniques.howItWorks: Drive a small set of named mix states off the sim's own intensity signal (inContact, recent fire density, casualties) and crossfade bus levels + HDR window params between them. CALM: wide window, atmos bus up, long reverb tail audible, near-total silence between events (the 'readable calm-before'). CONTACT: window narrows, combat bus forward, atmos pulled back, radio prioritized. OVERWHELM (heavy TIC / danger-close / IED): window very tight, atmos/score nearly gone, a low sub-floor (the tic_sting drone already exists) sustained — the world shrinks to the threat. States are a handful of target values you setTargetAtTime toward over ~1-3 s when the state changes; the transition itself is the drama. This is the somber-sim version of Battlefield's dynamic mix without any music stems.
techniques.webAudioMapping: A MixState enum -> {windowSize, releaseTau, atmosGain, combatGain, radioGain, scoreGain, subFloorGain}. Derive state in the mapper from inContact + a decaying fire-rate counter (pure, deterministic). On state change, the player ramps each bus.gain.setTargetAtTime(target, now, 1.5) and updates the HDR SIZE/releaseTau live. OVERWHELM also starts/sustains a 40-45 Hz sine on scoreBus (reuse the tic_sting drone) and shortens combat reverb wet. CALM raises atmosBus and the convolution wet so the valley breathes. No new node types — just scheduled gain targets keyed on a deterministic state signal.
techniques.source: DICE HDR 'dynamic mixing'; designingsound HDR writeup — https://designingsound.org/2013/06/21/finding-your-way-with-high-dynamic-range-audio-in-wwise/ ; existing tic_sting drone in lib/audio/synth.ts

techniques.name: Loudness targets & headroom for a somber war sim (LUFS/true-peak budget)
techniques.howItWorks: A somber sim wants WIDE dynamic range so the contrast between a held breath and an IED actually lands — chase quiet, broadcast/streaming-style targets, NOT loud-mobile-game targets. Reference points: EBU R128 -23 LUFS, console-game norm ~-24 LUFS (±2), Netflix cinematic -27 LUFS dialog-gated with a wide LRA. Treat the RADIO line as your 'dialog anchor' and mix everything else around it. Keep true-peak ceiling at -1 dBTP (the limiter enforces it). Generous headroom (peaks parked ~-6 dBFS in normal play) is what lets the IED actually feel +20 dB louder instead of just hitting the limiter the same as a rifle. This is the number that turns 'arcade loud' into 'documentary tense.'
techniques.webAudioMapping: Set DEFAULT_VOLUME so a typical firefight integrates around the equivalent of -24 LUFS at the user's reference and single rifle cracks peak ~-6 dBFS, leaving ~6 dB for blasts before the -1 dBTP limiter. Bus offsets implement the LRA: radioBus is the anchor (0 dB); atmos sits ~12-15 dB below combat in CALM so silence reads. Validate headlessly in scripts/audio-probe.ts by summing scheduled cue gains per frame (an OfflineAudioContext render + peak/RMS scan) and asserting the busiest frame stays under -1 dBTP and the calm/loud RMS spread is wide (>15 dB) — turns 'somber dynamic range' into a checkable number per the no-fix-without-a-number law.
techniques.source: vndev.wiki loudness guide (console -24, TP -1) — https://vndev.wiki/Guide:Balancing_a_Game's_Loudness ; Netflix/EBU cinematic targets — https://auphonic.com/blog/2020/10/08/dialog-loudness-normalization/ ; designingsound loudness ranges — https://designingsound.org/2013/02/20/different-loudness-ranges-for-console-and-mobile-games/

techniques.name: Blast 'deafening' duck + tinnitus tail (HDR window slam, dramatized)
techniques.howItWorks: When a near IED/large blast fires, momentarily slam the HDR window to its top and hard-duck every non-combat bus, then over ~1.5-3 s let it recover — the auditory equivalent of the over-pressure stun seen in Restrepo/The Outpost. A faint high sine 'ring' (tinnitus) fades in under the duck and out as the world returns. This is a single dramatic instance of the HDR mechanism, not a special case bolted on — it's the same window+duck machinery pushed to its extreme. Use sparingly (only near, large, player-relevant blasts) so it stays a gut-punch, not a gimmick.
techniques.webAudioMapping: On an ied/blast_large within audible radius: (1) force windowTop = blast loudness immediately (instant attack); (2) duck atmos/radio/score buses to ~0.15 with attackTau 0.004 then release over 1.5-3.0 s; (3) on scoreBus start a sine osc at ~4-6 kHz, gain ramp 0.0001->0.08 over 0.15 s then exponential decay over 2.5 s (tinnitus); (4) optionally drop combat-bus lowpass cutoff to ~1.5 kHz and ramp it back to 14 kHz over the recovery (muffled-then-clears). All deterministic: keyed on the blast cue id + its post-distance loudness threshold. Gate on distance so a far blast does NOT deafen.
techniques.source: DICE HDR (loudest sound moves window, quiet sounds vanish) — https://www.slideshare.net/aclerwall/how-high-dynamic-range-audio-makes-battlefield-bad-company-go-boom-1292018 ; tone references Restrepo/The Outpost; existing WaveShaper IED recipe in lib/audio/synth.ts

techniques.name: Procedural convolution reverb send per bus (valley tail, no asset)
techniques.howItWorks: The brief explicitly invites this: a ConvolverNode's impulse response can be PROCEDURALLY GENERATED (a decaying noise buffer), so we get convolution reverb with zero audio assets and no determinism break (the IR is built once render-side from generated noise, exactly like the existing shared noiseBuffer). A short, dark reverb tail on the COMBAT bus gives gunfire the canyon 'slap' that sells the Korengal valley — the single most identity-defining missing cue today (the spec notes 'NO reverb' currently). Keep it a parallel SEND (wet bus) scaled by distance/openness so close indoor-ish sounds stay dry and distant ridge fire blooms — and dial the wet down in CALM, up in CONTACT via the mix-state.
techniques.webAudioMapping: Build once: convolver = ctx.createConvolver(); convolver.buffer = a generated stereo IR — for i: ir[i] = (rand*2-1) * pow(1 - i/len, decayPow), len ~ 1.8s * sampleRate, decayPow ~2.5 for a dark canyon tail; optionally lowpass the IR samples for darkness. Wire as a SEND: combatBus -> wetSend(gain) -> convolver -> reverbReturn(gain) -> master, in parallel with the dry combatBus->master. Per-cue: scale wetSend contribution by distance (far ridge fire = more wet) — fold into schedule() alongside the existing pan/cutoff. Mix-state ramps reverbReturn.gain (CALM higher/longer-feeling, OVERWHELM lower/tighter). 100% procedural, deterministic IR, no file.
techniques.source: Web Audio ConvolverNode + procedural IR (brief-sanctioned) — https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio-1.1/ ; technique standard in Web Audio reverb tutorials — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/ConvolverNode

keyInsights: The whole axis collapses to ONE idea applied at three layers: the HDR auto-mixer. (a) compute-side: cue loudness in dB + a sliding window that the loudest sound raises and silence decays into; (b) voice-budget: priority-weighted stealing keeps nearest+loudest, drops quietest; (c) master: a DynamicsCompressorNode limiter as the dumb safety net. Build the window first — it gives legibility AND the 'readable calm-before' for free, because silence is just what the window decays to.

True audio-rate sidechain is impossible in vanilla Web Audio (DynamicsCompressorNode has no external trigger). The correct, cheap, DETERMINISTIC substitute is control-side ducking: ramp a BUS GainNode with setTargetAtTime when a trigger cue fires. Duck amount/timing is a pure function of which cue fired, so it stays inside the determinism contract — no AudioWorklet, no PRNG.

Prerequisite for everything: replace the single master GainNode with a 4-bus submix (combat/atmos/radio/score) -> master -> DynamicsCompressor limiter -> destination. Buses are the levers; without them, ducking and mix-states have nothing to grab. This is a small, surgical refactor of player.ts schedule().

The current 'drop the newest cue when over 24 voices' is backwards — it can mute the gunshot you need while a stale ricochet plays. Switch to priority-weighted stealing (DICE classes None/Low/Med/High/Permanent, tie-broken by post-HDR loudness) and raise the cap to ~32 now that HDR pre-culls and the limiter protects the sum.

Target QUIET, cinematic loudness (~-24 LUFS console / lean toward Netflix -27 dialog-gated, -1 dBTP ceiling, >15 dB calm-to-blast RMS spread). Wide dynamic range with generous headroom is the literal number that makes an IED feel +20 dB bigger than a rifle instead of both pinning the limiter — it's what turns 'arcade loud' into 'documentary tense'.

Two identity-defining gaps the spec flags as missing today are cheaply, asset-free closeable: a procedurally-generated ConvolverNode IR (decaying noise buffer) for the canyon reverb tail on the combat bus, and mix-states (calm/contact/overwhelm) crossfading bus levels + window params off the sim's own deterministic intensity signal.
pitfalls: Don't try to literally sidechain DynamicsCompressorNode — it has no external trigger input; reaching for an AudioWorklet to fake it adds CPU cost AND breaks determinism (worklet timing is wall-clock). Use control-side setTargetAtTime bus ducking instead.

Determinism break: any HDR window state / mix-state / duck timing that reads ctx.currentTime or Math.random in the DECISION layer violates Law 7. Keep the decision (loudness, window value, which bus ducks, mix-state) pure in the mapper; only the gain ramp's wall-clock anchor (now) lives in the player. The audio-probe must still get byte-identical cue+gain decisions for a seed.

Master limiter pumping: a too-aggressive DynamicsCompressorNode (high threshold, slow release) will audibly 'breathe' on every MG burst and flatten the somber dynamics you're trying to protect. Let per-cue HDR gains do the level work; keep the limiter as a conservative brickwall safety net with headroom (~-6 dBFS typical peaks), not the main mixer.

Arcade-y feel from over-ducking: if every radio squelch slams the whole mix, it reads as a video-game whoosh, not a field radio. Duck atmos a little and combat barely (or not at all) for radio; reserve the full-mix duck for genuine over-pressure (near large blast/IED) and use it RARELY so it stays a gut-punch.

Click/zipper noise: never step a bus or cue gain — always setTargetAtTime/exponentialRamp (the engine already does this for master; apply the same discipline to bus ducks and to torn-stolen voices via a 5 ms fade-to-0 before disconnect).

Killing the silence: an always-on ambient bed or a reverb tail that never decays would destroy the 'readable calm-before' that is a stated success criterion. The HDR window must be allowed to sink to near-silence between events; reverb wet and atmos must duck out in CALM, not drone.

Voice-steal thrash: stealing the lowest-priority voice every frame in a dense fight can cause audible chatter as voices are repeatedly killed mid-tail. Only steal when the incoming cue strictly outranks the live one, and prefer pre-culling at schedule time (HDR window bottom) over post-hoc stealing.

Mismeasuring success: verify the dynamic range and no-clip claims headlessly via an OfflineAudioContext render in audio-probe (peak/RMS per frame, busiest-frame true-peak < -1 dBTP, calm-vs-loud RMS spread > 15 dB) before declaring it improved — 'feels more immersive' is not a number.

techniques.name: Procedural valley reverb tail via ConvolverNode (decaying-noise IR)
techniques.howItWorks: A gunshot in a valley is a short muzzle blast followed by a long train of reflections off the far valley wall and ground — forensic-acoustics sources say a pop in a 'pristine environment' becomes 'a loud bang with reverberation lasting over a second' once surfaces are present (acoustics.org). James Moorer's classic result is that exponentially-decaying white noise makes a 'surprisingly good' reverb IR, so you can synthesize the entire valley tail with zero audio files. The valley signature is a LONG, BRIGHT-then-dark tail with discrete slap-back from the opposite ridge — not a smooth room. This is the single biggest missing piece: there is no reverb today and it is the #1 thing that will make a skeptic say 'they were there.'
techniques.webAudioMapping: Add a shared reverb send bus to player.ts (today the graph is cueGain->lp->pan->master with no send). Build the IR once with OfflineAudioContext(2, sampleRate*duration, sampleRate): fill both channels with white noise, multiply by an exp-decay envelope amp=pow(1-t/T, 2.2..3), bandpass-shape it (highpass ~250Hz + lowpass that sweeps from ~6kHz down to ~1.2kHz over the tail to model HF air-absorption of late reflections), and for the valley 'slap' add 1-2 discrete decaying noise bursts at ~0.18s and ~0.45s (path delay to the far wall ~30-80m round trip). Render -> ConvolverNode.buffer. Per-cue: split the wet send so you 'feed only the short snap into convolution' (Audiokinetic/Bungie) — wire the bright crack noiseBurst to convolver but NOT the sub body, so the tail rings without mud. Wet gain scales UP with distance norm (far events are almost all tail; near events are mostly dry). Decoupling the tail by environment/surface and EQ-ing the same source is exactly Bungie's Destiny approach.
techniques.source: Audiokinetic 'Outdoor Impulse Responses' + Bungie GDC 2015 (a decibel of difference recap, adbofdifference.com) + gskinner 'Making Reverb with the Web Audio API' + Moorer 'About This Reverberation Business'; acoustics.org forensic gunshot intro (reverberation 'lasting over a second')

techniques.name: HDR-style importance ducking (loud sounds suppress quiet ones)
techniques.howItWorks: Wwise HDR: the LOUDEST sounds define a moving window and automatically duck everything below it, so a machine gun 'effectively ducks down the volume of other less important sounds,' and relative levels are preserved to create the illusion of huge dynamic range inside the device's small range. For a SOMBER, restrained sim this is the core mechanism: when an IED goes off, the ambient bed, footsteps, distant pops, and radio all collapse for a beat — that collapse IS the visceral 'felt it' moment, achieved by making everything else quiet rather than the blast louder. It also keeps a 30-man firefight from clipping into arcade mush: only the few loudest events at any instant carry the mix.
techniques.webAudioMapping: Two compatible options. (A) Cheap/global: a master DynamicsCompressorNode (threshold ~-18dB, ratio ~6, attack 0.003s, release 0.25s, knee 6) so loud transients pull the whole mix down momentarily — preserves relative dynamics, prevents clip. (B) True HDR: a 'duck bus' for ambient+radio+small-arms; on scheduling a high-priority cue (ied/blast_large/dangerclose/tic_sting) call duckBus.gain.setTargetAtTime(0.35, now, 0.02) then setTargetAtTime(1.0, now+0.4, 0.35) — a programmatic sidechain keyed on cue priority rank, not amplitude detection (keeps it deterministic-friendly: the duck schedule is a pure function of the cue kind). Map KIND_TRIM priorities to duck depth. This is the 'silence as a musical thing' from Warfare implemented as gain automation.
techniques.source: Audiokinetic 'Wwise HDR: Overview and Best Practices'; designingsound.org 'Finding Your Way With High Dynamic Range Audio In Wwise'; A24 Warfare mix philosophy (post-super.com, screendaily)

techniques.name: Post-blast subjective tinnitus + muffle (the soldier's-ear POV)
techniques.howItWorks: The single most iconic war-film audio trope (Saving Private Ryan codified it): after a near explosion, the world drops to a muffled, low-passed roar overlaid with a steady high ringing tone, then slowly recovers. Warfare and All Quiet built their whole subjective approach on 'how each soldier perceived things... their own individual fog of war' and pulling sound 'inside the characters' minds.' For THIS sim the trigger is doctrinally clean: a danger-close fire mission landing, an IED, or a blast within N metres of the camera/friendly squad. Use it sparingly — overuse is 'one of the most overused tropes in film,' so gate it to genuinely close/large HE only, which keeps it grounded not Hollywood.
techniques.webAudioMapping: A subjective layer inserted on the MASTER chain (post-everything), engaged only on a close large-HE cue. Two parallel actions for a ~3-6s window: (1) a steady tinnitus tone — OscillatorNode sine at ~4-6kHz (+ a faint second at ~8kHz) through a gain that ramps in ~0.05s to a low level then decays over 4-8s; jitter its exact freq by cue.v for determinism. (2) a master 'ear-protect' lowpass — insert a BiquadFilter lowpass on the master bus, frequency.setValueAtTime(700, now) then exponentialRampToValueAtTime(14000, now+4..6) so the muffle lifts gradually; simultaneously duck master gain ~0.4 and ramp back. Optionally add a slow tremolo (gain LFO ~3-5Hz) for the 'underwater' pulse. Deterministic: trigger condition is a pure function of cue kind+distance; only the synth noise/osc is render-side.
techniques.source: No Film School 'Saving Private Ryan' sound story; movieweb (aural-trauma trope); Soundstripe 'All Quiet on the Western Front' (subjective soldier reality); A24 Warfare (individual fog of war, post-super.com)

techniques.name: Crack-thump distance cue — validate & extend (already partly built)
techniques.howItWorks: The supersonic bullet 'crack' (ballistic N-wave shockwave traveling with the round) arrives before the muzzle 'thump' (blast from the barrel), and the gap grows with distance: measured ~94ms at 50m and ~507ms at 300m — 'a perceptible time delay can give an experienced listener a rough indication of the distance of the firer.' The existing player.ts speed-of-sound split (343 m/s, split>0.08s) is CORRECT and matches the literature (the crack-thump is the most-cited 'sounds real' detail in every soldier account). The extension: the crack is a sharp, very-brief N-wave (high-frequency snap, ~1-2ms, only heard within the supersonic cone, i.e. when the round passes NEAR the listener), distinct from a distant report which is all thump and no crack.
techniques.webAudioMapping: Keep the existing crackAt/thumpAt scheduling — it's right. Two refinements: (1) The N-wave snap should be a bandpass 'tick' (~2-4kHz, ~12-20ms) only when the round actually passes near the camera (a true nearmiss), and the thump a separate lowpassed sub at the speed-of-sound delay — the current 'nearmiss' recipe and scheduleNearmissTail already model this; tighten the snap to ~2ms-attack/15ms-decay bandpass for the genuine N-wave bite. (2) For shots NOT passing near you (most of a firefight), suppress the crack entirely and play only the distance-delayed, lowpassed thump — distant fire is a soft, round 'pop...pop' with no snap. Gate snap-vs-thump on perpendicular distance from camera to the shot's line of fire, not just range.
techniques.source: Sciencedirect SA80 sound-exposure study & forensic gunshot acoustics (94ms@50m, 507ms@300m; N-wave heard only inside the cone, acoustics.org Beck); SoundCy gunshot-writing guide

techniques.name: Radio comms band-limited voice/squelch chain (proper lo-fi net)
techniques.howItWorks: Real combat-net traffic is its own emotional channel — Warfare's team built 'radio treatments with 100% accuracy... distortions designed to emulate the technical degradations' of comms, and 'radios flying around' carry the listener between silence and chaos. The recognised radio-effect chain is: steep highpass >500Hz + lowpass ~3kHz (telephone/PRC-148 band), mid-range SOFT saturation (not harsh distortion), heavy compression (e.g. ratio ~14, makeup ~+6dB), bracketed by squelch open/close noise bursts. The current 'radio' cue squelches but does NOT band-limit a voice element; making the net sound like a degraded speaker — even under a UI log line — is a huge presence win and reinforces 'you command, you don't shoot.'
techniques.webAudioMapping: Build a reusable radioVoice() sub-graph: source (a short formant-ish synth — 2-3 detuned saw/square OscillatorNodes through bandpass 'vowel' filters, OR just the existing squelch+beep) -> highpass BiquadFilter @ 500-600Hz, Q~0.7 -> lowpass @ 3kHz -> WaveShaper with a GENTLE tanh curve (drive ~1.3-1.8, the existing pattern) for grit -> DynamicsCompressor (threshold -30, ratio 12-14, attack 0.003, release 0.1) -> a peaking EQ +6dB @ ~1.5kHz for the 'speaker honk' -> ducked send to master. Top and tail with the existing open/close squelch noiseBursts. Keep KIND_TRIM.radio low so it sits UNDER the log line; route radio through the duck bus so HE collapses it too.
techniques.source: CRI Middleware 'Radio Voice Effect' blog + GameSalad/Cockos community chains (HP>500Hz, LP~3kHz, soft saturation, comp ratio ~14 +6dB); A24 Warfare radio treatment (post-super.com, screendaily)

techniques.name: Calm-before ambient bed + silence-as-contrast (the readable silence)
techniques.howItWorks: Restrepo/WAR is 'sound and fury broken by moments of unnerving stillness' — '100 miles per hour into a dead hole.' Warfare deliberately mixed non-battle scenes 'as quiet as we could make them without losing any detail,' using the DEPARTURE of an ambient (aircraft leaving, city falling silent) to create dread. Today the sim has NO ambient bed — silence is literally nothing, which reads as 'audio off' rather than 'tense calm.' A barely-there valley wind/insect/distant-stream bed makes silence ACTIVE; then HDR ducking yanks it away the instant contact starts, and its absence is what sells the violence. This is the single cheapest way to make the 'calm-before' a felt experience.
techniques.webAudioMapping: One persistent, looping ambient voice (NOT per-cue): a long looping AudioBufferSource of generated pink/brown noise -> a slowly-LFO'd lowpass (cutoff wandering 300-900Hz via a 0.05-0.2Hz LFO on frequency) for wind, + an optional faint high bandpass shimmer for insects at day, all at very low gain (~0.04-0.08) on the duck bus. Deterministic-safe: the bed loop is render-side noise, the LFO is wall-clock-free (driven by ctx time), and it emits no cues. On TIC rising edge (already detected in mapper -> tic_sting), ramp the bed gain to near-zero over ~0.3s; restore over several seconds when contact drops (respecting the existing one-way TIC latch caveat). Cross-fade bed character by World time-of-day/weather (wind louder in the existing weather state) for a living valley.
techniques.source: A24 Warfare (silence/ambient departure, post-super.com & televisual); Restrepo reception ('unnerving stillness', '100 mph into a dead hole', 500daysoffilm/IDA); BHD spectromorphology (pulsed desert wind, econtact.ca)

techniques.name: Spectral-reveal of distance (HF roll-off as a continuous distance axis)
techniques.howItWorks: Black Hawk Down opens with the helicopter 'high frequencies filtered out, then gradually reintroduced' — frequency content over time IS the distance/intimacy cue. Air absorption physically removes highs with distance (the late reverb tail also darkens), so a far PKM on the ridge is a dull thud while the same gun at the wire is a bright hammer. The existing air-absorption lowpass (12kHz near -> 700Hz far) is the right idea but is a single static value per cue; making it a true continuous, per-distance curve — and pairing it with the reverb wet/dry ratio rising with distance — gives one coherent 'how far' axis the listener reads unconsciously.
techniques.webAudioMapping: Refine the existing spatial() lowpass: keep cutoff = f(norm) but use a steeper perceptual mapping (e.g. cutoff = 14000 * pow(1-norm, 2.0), floor ~500Hz) AND a gentle high-shelf cut for additional darkness, not just one lowpass. Couple it: reverbWetGain = norm (far = mostly tail), dryGain = (1-norm)*0.6+0.4. For the elevation cue this axis is missing today — add a SMALL high-shelf boost for shots from above the camera's terrain elevation (the ridge gun 'rings' more openly) vs a muffled low-shelf for shots from defilade/below; read elevation from the existing 512x512 elevation grid at cue.pos. Subtle (a few dB) — grounded, not gimmicky.
techniques.source: Black Hawk Down spectromorphology analysis (econtact.ca, Gates/Rudy); standard air-absorption acoustics; Audiokinetic outdoor-IR HF-decay notes

techniques.name: Directional intent — 'every snap is very directional' (tighten panning)
techniques.howItWorks: Warfare's Ray Mendoza: 'every snap, every round has a purpose... when there's a snap, it's very directional,' and the core dramatic problem of a firefight is 'identifying where fire originates' amid 'confusion.' The gameplay payoff is huge: if the player can HEAR which direction incoming is coming from (left ridge vs right village), the top-down tactical read becomes audible. The current StereoPanner uses screen-x only; that's correct for a top-down camera but can be sharpened and made the deliberate carrier of tactical information (enemy fire panned hard to its bearing; friendly outgoing centered/softer).
techniques.webAudioMapping: Keep StereoPanner (top-down 2D — full HRTF PannerNode is overkill and CPU-heavy at 24 voices). Sharpen the existing screen-x pan: widen the pan law so off-center events reach |0.7-1.0| sooner (events near screen edge should feel clearly L/R), and slightly REDUCE pan width for friendly/outgoing muzzle cues so YOUR squad feels 'with you' (centered) while ENEMY fire is panned hard to its bearing — leveraging the existing muzzle_us vs muzzle_insurgent split. Add a tiny inter-aural delay (DelayNode 0-0.6ms by sign of pan) for extra directional bite if cheap. This makes bearing-to-threat audible, the tactical-read win.
techniques.source: SlashFilm A24 Warfare interview (Ray Mendoza, 'very directional', 'where fire originates'); indiewire Warfare sound interview

keyInsights: The #1 gap vs real valley combat is REVERB: a Korengal shot is mostly its tail bouncing off the far ridge. A procedurally-generated decaying-noise impulse response in a ConvolverNode (Moorer's method, zero audio files) is fully allowed and is the highest-leverage single addition. Feed only the bright SNAP into the convolver (not the sub body) to get a ringing valley tail without mud — Bungie's and Audiokinetic's exact technique.

SOMBER comes from DYNAMICS, not from making things loud. HDR-style ducking — the loudest event momentarily collapses ambient/radio/small-arms — is how Warfare makes an IED 'felt': silence around the blast, not a louder blast. Implement as a deterministic duck bus keyed on cue PRIORITY (pure function of cue kind), plus a gentle master compressor to stop a 30-man fight from clipping into arcade mush.

The existing crack-thump speed-of-sound split is acoustically CORRECT (literature: ~94ms@50m, ~507ms@300m) and is the most-cited 'this sounds real' detail in every soldier account — don't rebuild it, refine it: a true N-wave snap ONLY when the round passes near the listener, otherwise pure delayed thump for distant fire.

Make SILENCE active. There is no ambient bed today, so 'calm-before' reads as 'audio off.' A barely-there wind/valley bed (looping generated noise + slow LFO'd lowpass) that HDR-ducks to near-zero on the TIC rising edge turns silence into dread — Restrepo's 'unnerving stillness', Warfare's 'as quiet as we could make them.'

Subjective player-ear POV (post-blast tinnitus + lifting lowpass muffle on the master bus) is the iconic war-film move and maps cleanly to a deterministic trigger (close large-HE / danger-close only). Gate it tightly — it's 'one of the most overused tropes in film', so rare use keeps it grounded, not Hollywood.

Architecture seam: today the graph is per-cue gain->lowpass->pan->master with a single bus. Realizing reverb + HDR ducking + the ambient bed needs a few SHARED buses (dry, reverb-send/convolver, duck-bus, subjective master insert). This is additive and stays render-side; the mapper/cue layer remains pure — only synth.ts/player.ts grow. Distance should drive ONE coherent axis: HF roll-off + reverb wet/dry ratio + (subtle) elevation shelf together = 'how far / how high'.
pitfalls: Reverb mud: feeding the FULL designed shot (sub body + tail) into the convolver smears the low end into a roar. Feed only the short bright snap/spike into the IR (Audiokinetic/Bungie); keep the sub dry. Also cap convolver wet on near events — close shots are mostly dry.

Hollywood-bombastic overload: do NOT make blasts louder to feel powerful — that's arcade. Power comes from ducking everything ELSE (HDR). Resist constant musical stings; tic_sting is the ONLY musical element and must stay rare and gated to the TIC rising edge.

Tinnitus trope abuse: triggering the ringing/muffle on every blast is cliché and exhausting ('most overused trope in film'). Gate to genuinely close + large HE / danger-close only, a handful of times per engagement.

Determinism break: ConvolverNode IRs, ambient bed loops, and tinnitus oscillators MUST live render-side (player.ts/synth.ts) and never feed lib/sim. The duck schedule and tinnitus TRIGGER must be pure functions of cue kind/distance (no amplitude-following analyser, no Math.random in the trigger) so the cue->behavior mapping stays deterministic; only the noise/osc samples themselves are render-side, exactly like the existing noiseBuffer.

CPU/polyphony: a single ConvolverNode with a 1.5-3s IR shared across all sends is cheap; do NOT create a convolver per cue. Avoid full HRTF PannerNode per voice (overkill for top-down 2D and heavy at the 24-voice cap) — StereoPanner is correct here. Build the IR once via OfflineAudioContext at unlock, not per frame.

Stale/over-long tails in a sustained firefight: a 3s valley tail on every one of hundreds of rounds will pile up and smear into white noise. Send only a fraction of cues (e.g. the loudest / most distant) to reverb, scale wet by distance, and let the polyphony cap + HDR duck thin it — the goal is the OCCASIONAL ridge-echo, not a wash.

Don't conflate 'slow/quiet' with 'broken': the readable silence is a FEATURE (no events => no sound is correct). The ambient bed must be barely audible (~0.04-0.08 gain) and must not become a constant drone that erases the calm-vs-contact contrast.
